questions.question: What motivated you to go on exchange? (pick the most important one) *
questions.answer: Academic opportunities

questions.question: Which aspects were crucial to choosing your study destination? *
questions.answer: NUS is a leading and well-known university and I wanted to spend my exchange challenging myself both academically and personally. Singapore itself intrigued me as a place to live, as it is highly culturally diverse and as a city is fundamentally different from many other places in the world with its architecture, fast pace and futuristic vibe.

questions.question: How would you rate your overall study abroad experience? *
Additional comments:
How easy was it to find the information you needed to know upon arrival? *
questions.answer: When you receive the application material from NUS (for me, it was around June/July, and I was attending the spring semester), the university sends several PDFs that include step-by-step guides on how to apply to the university, choose courses, apply for a visa, student accommodation, etc. After you’ve been officially enrolled, they also host a webinar where they go through many of the details. There was a lot of material from NUS, but it was easy to understand and navigate. Before I received anything from NUS (which happens gradually over a few months, depending on the steps), I found it really difficult to get information through KU, so you have to be patient and wait for NUS to contact you directly.

questions.question: What assistance, if any, did you receive when you arrived at your study destination? *
questions.answer: Most of the assistance I received was through the documents sent by NUS. They send a lot of emails and reminders about where, when, and how to complete the various administrative steps when you arrive, such as getting your student card, sorting out your visa, and knowing which documents to bring. These procedures take place in a gym on campus. I stayed in one of the residence halls, and the staff there were also very helpful. NUS also has several of their own apps, for example, uNivUS, which serves as your school calendar and contains a lot of information in one place. Since you receive so much information, I recommend reading it carefully because they expect you to know the details, deadlines, and other important information stated in the documents.

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the orientation and assistance available to students at your host institution upon arrival? *
Additional comments
questions.answer: I was very satisfied with all the information I received from NUS, but it was also stressful because there was a lot of administrative work to do both before and after my arrival in Singapore, with little support to help ensure you complete everything before the deadlines.

questions.question: How did you find housing? *
questions.answer: I found housing through my host institution

questions.question: Did you live on campus or off campus? *
questions.answer: On campus

questions.question: What options were available for on campus housing? *
questions.answer: NUS offers many different on-campus housing options, which are quite similar to college life in the US. You live with students from all over the world studying a variety of degrees. There are lots of hawker centres (food courts), school canteens, gyms, infinity pools, libraries, cafes, and sports facilities like tennis courts, swimming pools, and bouldering, all within walking distance or accessible by free buses that run across campus. Some residences offer private rooms without meal plans, and some include air conditioning (I can recommend Utown Residence). There are also colleges and halls with meal plans that usually include breakfast and dinner. Typically, you can have your own room, though in some colleges you share a flat with 4-5 other students. I recommend the College of Alice and Peter Tan (CAPT) (as a second priority after Utown Residence), where you get your own room and a meal plan - though unfortunately, air conditioning is not available there, which can be hard to find on campus.

questions.question: What options were available for meal plans or cooking facilities? *
questions.answer: Meal plans are very common. I only know of Utown Residence as an exception, it doesn’t have meal plans, so students living there usually buy their food from the hawker centers in Utown. Cooking facilities are not common and if they are provided, they are not very well equipped.

questions.question: What should future exchange students know about living in on campus housing? *
questions.answer: I can only recommend living on campus because it’s such a unique experience, you get to meet many other exchange and local students, and it’s fun to live in the campus environment that NUS offers. Apply to Utown since it’s very popular, just apply to everything you can and try to get a room with AC, though that can be difficult. I lived at Kent Ridge Hall, which didn’t have AC and was located outside Utown. The meal plan wasn’t great, but it was okay for those four months because it was very social. However, everyone had problems with mold due to the humidity and having only a ceiling fan. If you get a room without AC, I recommend buying a humidifier.

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the housing available to students? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: Don't apply to Kent Ridge Hall or any of the other halls located outside Utown. Don't apply to PCGP, it is far away.

questions.question: How easy did you find the registration process at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
Please describe the registration process at your host institution *
questions.answer: NUS sends you a step-by-step guide on how to apply for courses. The application is done through their own system and takes place at the same time as enrollment. The process is very easy, you just have to prioritize 7-10 different courses. I recommend using NUSMods to get an overview of the schedule. After classes begin, you have the chance to change courses during weeks 1-3, and that process is also quite easy. So if you attend a class and realize it’s not the right fit, you can apply for a different course.

questions.question: What kind of help was available? *
questions.answer: There was no help from KU and only limited help from NUS beyond the guides provided in their documents. I talked a lot with others who were also going to Singapore during the application process.

questions.question: How successful were you in registering for the classes you wanted? *
questions.answer: I almost got all of the classes I applied for.

questions.question: What advice would you offer to future exchange students about registration at your host institution? *
questions.answer: Be sure to meet NUS's deadlines. They are quite strict, and if you miss them, you risk not getting the courses you want, as you'll have to wait for later application rounds.

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the academic programme at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
Were you a BA or MA student at UCPH when you were on exchange? *
questions.answer: MA

questions.question: Did you take BA or MA classes while you were on exchange *
questions.answer: MA

questions.question: Please elaborate on the level of courses *
questions.answer: You attend classes with a mix of bachelor’s, master’s, and LLM students, so the level among students varies quite a bit, but you won’t be evaluated the same way as, for example, LLM students.

questions.question: How did the style of teaching at your host institution compare with that of UCPH? *
questions.answer: The teaching style is very different from KU. At NUS you are required and expected to attend and participate in class as a part of your grade (between 10-30% comes from class participation). However, the professors are very welcoming and eager to hear the students’ input and the learning environment is quite good. The approach is also more theoretical. NUS focuses more on discussing the theory and reasoning behind the rules, judgments, and articles, rather than simply learning how to apply them as you do at KU.

questions.question: How long were you on exchange? *
questions.answer: 1 semester

questions.question: Please list the courses you were enrolled in during your first semester. *
questions.answer: World Trade Law (5 units), Global Data Protection Law (5 units), Foundations of IP Law (5 units), Intellectual Property and Human Rights (4 units).

questions.question: What specific courses would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer: I would recommend World Trade Law and Global Data Privacy Law. There’s a LOT of reading in World Trade Law throughout the semester, but it’s very up-to-date with the current situation between the US and China, and you’ll gain a solid understanding of the legal instruments related to trade. Global Data Privacy Law is a very interesting course where you study UK, US, and EU privacy laws from a comparative perspective. There’s a lot of class discussion, for example, on the clash between privacy and new technologies. It’s a great course to take at NUS because the students come from all over the world, which makes the discussions even more interesting. Plus, the professor is brilliant.

What unexpected costs did you encounter? *
questions.answer: Transportation is important to consider since the campus is a bit outside Singapore’s city center. Public transport is very cheap, but using Grab is often easier and faster—especially at night when public transportation doesn’t run after midnight. However, Grab can be more expensive during those hours.

questions.question: What items were more or less expensive than you expected? *
questions.answer: Food was less expensive than I expected. It’s very cheap to eat at the hawker centres both in and outside the city center, as well as in the canteens on campus.

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the non-academic opportunities (clubs, sports, etc.) at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: UTown is a great place to meet up spontaneously in the evenings. It has restaurants and hawker centres, nice outdoor areas to hang out, libraries, infinity pools, and a free gym that’s open 24/7. There’s Wi-Fi everywhere. You can also do various sports like tennis, swimming, bouldering, volleyball, and even go hiking around the campus area.

questions.question: What kinds of cultural, athletic and social activities were available for students at your host institution? *
questions.answer: NUS hosts many events throughout the semester for exchange students. There are also plenty of sports clubs you can join. I recommend applying for the NUS Buddy Programme. I had a Singaporean buddy who also studied law, and he was a huge help. He answered all my questions about NUS, gave me great insider tips about Singapore, and we went on hikes and did other activities together.

questions.question: Which non -academic activities would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer: Spend the days and weekends to experience Singapore. Some of the best places are: the Botanical Garden, Gardens by the Bay and the lightshow, the two domes in Gardens by the Bay, Chinatown and Outram, Merlion, Sentosa, hike at Henderson Waves, Southern Ridges and Macritchie Reservoir, Ce La Vie (Nightclub, ladies night every Wednesday, free entrance), La Pau Sat (Hawkercenter in the city center), Boat Quay (good place for beers in the evenings), Haji Lane, Art Science Museum, Singapore Sling at Raffles Hotel.

questions.question: What do you recommend other visiting students see or do on their weekends or holidays? *
questions.answer: Go to Johor Bahru and Kuala Lumpur in Malaysia and travel around Asia if you have the time. Or experience Singapore.

questions.question: How easy was it to adjust to the local culture of your exchange site? *
questions.answer: It was very easy to adjust as everything is in English. Even though the culture differs a bit from what I'm used to, it was easy to settle into because Singapore is so diverse and people are used to meeting people from all over the world. The whole infrastructure is also designed for international purposes.

questions.question: Do you have any tips for socializing with local students?
questions.answer: Apply for a local buddy because that is the easiest way to get to know the local students. Apply for on-campus housing on because almost all of the local students live on campus so that's a great way to meet them. Also, try to be social in the breaks during class because in my experience the locals are very interested in getting to know exchange students.

questions.question: What, if any, cultural differences did you find particularly challenging? *
questions.answer: Singapore has a lot of rules you need to be aware of to avoid getting fined. For example, you’re not allowed to drink water on public transportation, and you have to wave to signal the bus to stop for you.

questions.question: What parts of the culture did you most appreciate? *
questions.answer: Singapore has so many great qualities. The people are respectful and welcoming, everything is well-organized and efficient, it’s clean, easy to get around, and there’s a lot to experience, both culturally, city and nightlife and in terms of nature. The weather is also quite nice. You can also get food from all over Asia in the Hawker Centers for no money, and some of them are on the Michelin Guide. I can really recommend trying that.

questions.question: What are the three most important things you would tell a UCPH student who is going to your host institution on exchange? *
questions.answer: 1) Don’t get too intimidated or stressed by how formal and strict NUS may seem in writing. It feels much more relaxed once you’re actually in Singapore. 2) Don’t worry too much about the participation requirement. As long as you attend most classes and contribute a few times during the semester, you’ll be fine. 3) Make sure to experience Singapore itself. Not just use it as a base for traveling. There's so much to explore locally.

questions.question: Is there any other information that you think might prove useful to future exchange students attending your host institution? *
questions.answer: Make sure to read all the material you receive from NUS before going and make sure to meet their deadlines.

questions.question: What was the most rewarding part of your exchange experience? *
questions.answer: I grew a lot both academically and personally during my time in Singapore. NUS is truly an excellent university. The professors, courses, reading materials, and fellow students are all fantastic. Although there’s quite a bit of administrative work involved in preparing to go to Singapore, it’s definitely worth it once you arrive. I can’t recommend it enough.

questions.question: What was the greatest challenge during the exchange? *
questions.answer: To keep up with all of the readings while prioritizing social activities throughout the semester. Live at a dorm without AC.

questions.question: Any other comments?
Do you agree to share your travel report with other fellow students? *
questions.answer: Yes
